content: A breech presentation occurs when a baby’s buttocks are positioned lower than the baby’s head within the mother’s uterus, leading to the buttocks being delivered before the head during childbirth. This condition is observed in approximately 3% to 4% of singleton births and is associated with an increased risk of complications during delivery, including a higher likelihood of cesarean sections. It is generally considered preferable to attempt to turn the baby into a head-down position before labor begins, provided the procedures used do not result in significant adverse effects. Acupuncture has been proposed as a potential method for correcting breech presentation. Acupuncture involves the therapeutic insertion of solid needles at specific meridian points on the body, following various patterns and combinations. Factors that predispose to breech presentation include uterine malformations, placenta previa, prematurity, polyhydramnios, multiple gestations, and fetal anomalies. In 2000, the Term Breech Trial demonstrated that elective cesarean sections reduced infant morbidity and mortality compared to planned vaginal delivery for breech presentations. Since then, cesarean sections have become the standard practice for term breech presentations in many Western countries. However, turning a breech baby before labor remains a preferred approach. Several treatment modalities have been proposed to address breech presentation, including external cephalic version, postural management, moxibustion, moxibustion combined with acupuncture, and expedited delivery. Acupuncture can be used to treat specific symptoms or conditions, either in a standardized manner or individualized to the patient’s constitution and specific needs. The treatment can vary in terms of the acupuncture points used, the type of needles, and the number and duration of sessions. Techniques such as auricular acupuncture, electro-acupuncture, moxibustion, heat application, and laser acupuncture are often employed to enhance the therapeutic effect. Acupuncture is practiced worldwide by a variety of professionals, including Western medicine-trained physicians, Eastern medicine-trained physicians, licensed acupuncturists, chiropractors, and physical therapists. Standards for reporting acupuncture interventions in clinical trials have been developed, such as the STRICTA guidelines, which extend the CONSORT guidelines for clinical trial reporting. Specific acupuncture points, such as LI4, ST36, and SP6, have been implicated in the treatment of fetal malposition during pregnancy. The mechanism by which acupuncture may work is hypothesized to involve the stimulation of biochemical cascades, including hormonal changes mediated through ascending neuronal pathways to the hypothalamus or reflex activation of autonomic efferent nerves to the uterus. Acupuncture may also increase adrenocortical activity and alter the prostaglandin F2alpha to prostaglandin E2 ratio, which can raise uterine basal tone and enhance contractility. The use of sham acupuncture as a control in studies is controversial, as it does not provide a truly inert placebo-controlled comparison. Needling, whether superficial or deep, at acupuncture or non-acupuncture sites, induces physiological responses, including analgesic effects, changes in microcirculation, and diffuse noxious inhibitory control. The close-knit nature of acupuncture meridians and their potential overlap complicates the use of sham techniques. Additionally, blinding of the acupuncturist is not feasible, as trained practitioners can distinguish between true acupuncture and sham techniques. This limitation may introduce bias, such as the Rosenthal Effect, where outcomes align with the experimenter’s expectations. Acupuncture is increasingly integrated into Western medicine, with growing demand from patients. For example, around two million Americans reported recent use of acupuncture in the 2002 US National Health Interview Survey. In the UK, organizations like the British Medical Acupuncture Society have promoted its use. Acupuncture is also widely practiced in Europe, Asia, and other parts of the world. However, it is still often regarded as complementary or alternative to conventional modern medicine. This review aims to evaluate studies that use acupuncture to turn a breech presentation. It will include any studies involving acupuncture needles, regardless of the specific points or types of needles used, and whether additional modalities like electricity, laser, or heat were applied. Acupuncture combined with moxibustion is covered in a separate Cochrane review and will not be included here.
